sweep_summary: The search of works with stress or accent in the title for kabu1256 (Kabuverdianu, catalog classification lexical, deciding source Lang et al. 2018 Gramática do Crioulo da ilha de Santiago §1.3.2.1/§1.3.2.2.3) turned up exactly one title-keyword hit: Andrade, Gomes & Teixeira 1992, 'Observações sobre o sistema acentual do crioulo da Guiné-Bissau (CGB)', Actas do colóquio sobre crioulos de base lexical portuguesa pp. 135-140 (Colibri, Lisbon). It is about Guinea-Bissau Creole (Kriyol), not Kabuverdianu; Glottolog's own record marks the kea language code as a computerized assignment from the word 'crioulo' (Maho's eballiso2009 entry, keyword gnb). No open copy was found (archive.org 0 hits, Crossref no match, Google Books no items; Priority for acquisition: none for this language. No new first-hand stress statement for Kabuverdianu was read in this search of works with stress in the title, so no new stress statement was found and the catalog's deciding source (Lang et al. 2018, held at and previously quote-checked) stands unchanged. Earlier check downloads already held by the project in (Tavares Moreira 2020 Fogo thesis, 'refines'; Freitas 2018 RILP, 'silent') were not part of this title search's item list and are unchanged. Saved this search of works with stress in the title: plus a line in that directory.

new_statements.quote: Em primeiro lugar, o acento é distintivo no Caboverdiano, e ele não ocupa uma posição fixa em todos os vocábulos. Essa é uma língua de acento livre: ele pode flutuar e incidir na última, penúltima ou antepenúltima sílaba. E, assim, o vocábulo pode ser oxítono, paroxítono ou proparoxítono. Como acontece na maioria das línguas do mundo, o acento paroxítono é o não-marcado nas quatro ilhas. O acento proparoxítono é o marcado por ser mais extenso e menos usual nas ilhas. O acento oxítono, preponderante em Barlavento, é considerado mais marcado que o paroxítono e menos marcado que o proparoxítono. [p. 211] — Em Santiago, o verbo dissilábico apresenta um padrão categoricamente paroxítono, troqueu. [p. 186]
new_statements.translation: First, stress is distinctive in Cape Verdean, and it does not occupy a fixed position in all words. This is a free-stress language: it can float and fall on the last, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. And so a word can be oxytone, paroxytone or proparoxytone. As in most of the world's languages, paroxytone (penultimate) stress is the unmarked one in the four islands. Proparoxytone stress is the marked one, being longer and less usual in the islands. Oxytone stress, predominant in Barlavento, is considered more marked than paroxytone and less marked than proparoxytone. [p. 211] — In Santiago, the disyllabic verb shows a categorically paroxytone, trochaic pattern. [p. 186]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for kabu1256 has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so there is nothing to agree with or contradict; this work supplies the first placement statement: free/contrastive stress with penultimate default, final stress with final liquid/nasal, and a Santiago-specific categorical penultimate pattern in regular verbs.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive and not fixed: it may fall on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, so the position must be known per word. Penultimate stress is the unmarked default in all four islands studied (Santiago, Fogo, Santo Antão, São Vicente); final stress is common (predominant in the northern Barlavento islands) and antepenultimate stress is rare and marked. Predictable subpatterns: in Santiago, regular (disyllabic) verbs are categorically penultimate/trochaic (p. 186; 'Nos verbos, o padrão pararoxítono é encontrado somente em Sotavento', p. 194), whereas in Santo Antão and São Vicente regular verbs are oxytone and Fogo alternates (p. 187); the author endorses Veiga (1996:105) that Cape Verdean stress 'é, largamente, de natureza paroxítona' but a final liquid (or nasal) consonant 'indica preditibilidade oxítona' (p. 188), and her OT analysis uses WSP, i.e. a final heavy (closed) syllable attracts stress. Open mid vowels /ɛ, ɔ/ are always stressed (p. 211).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not analysed by the author. She only quotes Lopes da Silva (1957:35), who explained the retraction of stress in Santiago oxytone disyllabic verbs (fika for fikâ, perde for perdê) 'pela valorização de um acento secundário incidente na sílaba inicial' — a hypothesis Lopes da Silva himself called obscure (p. 227).
new_statements.exceptions: Irregular verbs keep the same stress in all islands (éra, kumeba; p. 187, citing Veiga 1998:107); Fogo verbs oscillate between penult and final (nxina~nxinâ, kume~kumê; p. 186); proparoxytones such as fábrika, mákina, prósimu, últimu occur in all four islands but are rare and marked (pp. 200-201, 207); a Lang (1994a, 1999) morphophonological alternation in Santiago distinguishes verbs from nouns by the height of the stressed mid vowel (kareka 'go bald' vs karéka 'bald'; p. 205), not by stress position.
new_statements.identity_note: Souza 2007 describes four island varieties — Santiago and Fogo (Sotavento) and Santo Antão and São Vicente (Barlavento) — from 2001/2002 fieldwork; the p. 211 generalization is stated for all four islands, while the categorical penultimate verb pattern (p. 186, p. 194) is specific to Santiago (and, less consistently, Fogo), which is the variety the catalog item names (santiaguense). The Barlavento oxytone verb pattern does not apply to Santiago.
